Run both against the same log. ^Gzip finishes in a second, giving six megabytes. ^B zip two takes eight and a half, giving four and a half. You're paying ^seven times the processor time for a megabyte and a half. Whether that's worth it depends on what happens next. ^For a log you rotate nightly, it's a waste. ^For an archive you keep for seven years, it's obviously right. ^Write once, read almost never, is where it pays. ^X Z goes further still. ^But gzip stays the default, because it's fast enough and ^always installed. ~Match the compressor to how often you pay the cost back. Gzip for anything you touch often, bzip2 or xz for anything you're storing and forgetting.
headline: bzip2 trades [time] for size

narration: You've an archive which needs to go to somebody who has quite honestly never opened a terminal window in their entire life. |Zip is what they can open, and the difference from tar dot gz is structural. ^A tar dot gz is a single compressed stream, so ^to reach one file in the middle you've to decompress everything before it. ^Zip compresses each file separately ^and keeps an index at the end of the archive. That means you can ^pull one file straight out without touching the rest. ^And it opens with a double click on any operating system. ~So the rule is really about who opens it. Send zip to people and tar dot gz to servers.
headline: zip is the [portable] one

narration: Scheduling on Linux comes down to one line of five numbers, and almost everybody copies that line from somewhere else without ever reading it properly. |Cron is five fields in a fixed order, and that order is the whole trick. ^The first field is the minute, zero to fifty nine. ^The second is the hour, zero to twenty three. ^The third is the day of the month. ^The fourth is the month. ^The fifth is the day of the week, where zero is Sunday. Then ^a star simply means every one of whatever that field counts. So this line means ^half past two in the morning, on Mondays only. ~Five stars means every single minute of every day, which is how people take servers down by accident. Read the five fields left to right, and any cron line becomes plain English.
headline: cron is [five fields]

narration: Cron is the schedule; |crontab is how you edit it. ^Dash E opens your table in an editor, and the important bit is that ^it validates the file when you save. ^A syntax error is rejected there and then, with a message telling you. Now compare that with editing the crontab file directly on disk, which people do all the time. ^That skips the check completely, and ^cron will simply skip the broken job, silently, forever. No email, no log entry, nothing. Which is why |dash ^L matters: it prints what's actually loaded right now, and ^that's the only real proof your job exists. ~A schedule you never verified isn't a schedule. Always use crontab dash E, then crontab dash L to confirm what actually got installed.
headline: crontab -e, never [edit the file]

narration: A script is just a file with commands in it, and yet |the first time you run one you get ^permission denied. Here's why. ^New files aren't created executable, because which would be a terrible default. So |change mod plus X ^flips exactly that one bit, and ^the very same command now works. Two more details. ^The first line of the script names the interpreter that should run it, and ^that line is called the shebang. And |you ^have to write dot slash in front of the name, because the current folder is deliberately not in your search path. ~That's a security decision: if it were, dropping a file called L S into a shared directory would hijack everyone's commands. Shebang, chmod plus X, then dot slash. Three things, and your script runs anywhere.
headline: Three lines and a [permission bit]

narration: |Alias binds a long command to a short name, and the trap is about where that binding lives. ^Type it at the prompt and it works straight away, ^but only inside this one shell, and only until you close it. ^Open a new terminal and it has gone. If you want it to outlive the session, |append it to ^your bashrc, which every new shell reads on startup, and ^now it survives forever. But here's the one which catches people. ^A script still can't see your aliases, ^because a script runs a non-interactive shell and bashrc isn't read at all. ~Which is exactly why a command that works perfectly when you type it fails the moment cron runs the same line. Put your aliases in bashrc, and put the real command in your scripts.
headline: An alias dies unless you [save it]

narration: |Env shows the variables a command inherits when it starts. ^Path tells the shell where to look for commands. ^Home is your home directory. And ^every process you start inherits a copy of this whole set, which is how configuration reaches a program without a config file. Now the genuinely useful trick here. |Put ^debug equals one in front of a command and you've set that variable ^for that process alone, and for anything it starts. ^The very next command you type has no debug at all. ^Nothing else on the machine ever saw it. ~That matters on a shared box, because exporting a secret into your shell leaves it sitting in the environment of everything you run afterwards. Setting a variable in front of a command is the safest way to try something once.
headline: env changes it for [one command]

narration: |History keeps ^everything you've typed, numbered, and there are three ways to reach back into it. ^Bang followed by a number runs that exact line again. |Bang ^bang runs the previous command. And the one you'll genuinely use every day is this: you run something, it fails because it needed privilege, and rather than retype any of it you just run |sudo ^bang bang. Better still, ^control R searches backwards through your history as you type. One warning, though. ^All of this is written to a file in your home directory, ^so any password you ever typed as part of a command is sitting on disk in plain text. ~Which is a good reason never to put one on a command line. Sudo bang bang will save you more typing this year than any other two words here.
headline: history plus [Ctrl-R]

narration: Start a long job over S S H and it dies when the connection drops, because ^your session belongs to that connection and ^when it closes, everything inside goes with it. |Screen fixes that properly. ^Dash capital S creates a session which lives on the server itself, and ^the job runs inside that session rather than inside your connection. So now ^your connection can drop, your laptop can sleep, and the work carries straight on. When you come back, |screen ^dash R reattaches you and everything is exactly where you left it. And ^control A then D detaches deliberately. ~The session belongs to the server, not to you, which is the whole point. Start anything long inside screen or tmux, and a dropped connection stops mattering.
headline: screen survives your [dropped wifi]

narration: |T mux does everything screen does, so you get ^the same survival across a dropped connection, ^and then T mux splits the terminal into panes. That sounds cosmetic until you use it. ^One pane holds your editor. ^Another holds the logs, live, as you work. ^T mux's one session holding both, so you're watching your change and its effect at the same time without switching windows. |Attach ^by name from any machine and the whole layout comes back. One practical note: ^control B is the prefix key for everything in T mux, where screen uses control A. ~The muscle memory doesn't transfer between them, so pick one and commit to it. Tmux is worth an afternoon of practice, because it changes how you work on servers.
headline: tmux adds [panes] to the same idea

narration: Here's the distinction which catches people out, and getting the two confused costs them an outage. A service has ^two separate switches, not one. Here it's stopped. |Start it and ^it's running right now, serving traffic, completely fine. ^But it'll not come back after a reboot, because that's the other switch. |Enable is the one that ^makes it start at boot, and it doesn't start it now. So ^reboot this machine and ^only the service you enabled comes back on its own. |Status ^shows you both states at once, which is why it's the command to run when something isn't behaving. ~You almost always want both, and enable dash dash now does the pair in one go. Systemctl enable dash dash now is the command you actually wanted, nearly every time.
headline: start is now. [enable] is after reboot

narration: The mistake with |journal C T L is treating it like a file and scrolling. ^Journal C T L's a database, and you query it. ^Dash U narrows to one service, which is usually the first thing you want. |Add ^dash B and you only see this boot, so yesterday's noise disappears. Add ^dash P err and you only see errors and worse. ^Three filters, and what's left is the thing you were looking for. And when you want to watch it happen, |dash ^F follows the journal live, exactly like tail dash F on a log file. ~The habit worth building is ^composing filters rather than scrolling, because every flag narrows the set and they stack. Compose the filters and journalctl goes from overwhelming to the fastest log tool you own.
headline: journalctl is [filters], not scrolling

narration: When a piece of hardware starts to fail, the kernel notices it long before anything gets written down in a log file anywhere. The command is |D mesg, and D mesg prints ^that buffer, which isn't a log file at all. ^D mesg's fixed in size and it's a ring, which means ^new messages come in one end and ^the oldest are pushed off the other and lost. ^Dash T makes timestamps readable; by default they're seconds since boot. Now why you care: ^a disk starting to fail, a cable going bad, memory throwing errors, all of it appears here first, ^long before anything writes it to a log file. ~So check it early. On a busy machine that buffer wraps, and the message that explained everything is simply gone. Dmesg dash T piped into tail is worth running whenever a machine behaves strangely.
headline: dmesg is a [ring buffer]

narration: Quick one. You |started a service, and a reboot killed it. What was missed? Have a think, and pause here if you need longer. |Ready? Enable, not just start.

quiz.question: Service works, dies after reboot. Missed what?
quiz.why: start runs it now. enable is what survives a reboot.

narration: Drawer nine runs without you. |Tar and gzip package it. |Cron schedules it. |System C T L and journal C T L supervise it. |T mux keeps it alive while you sleep.
Drawer ten. What to do when you're stuck, which is why these exist.

The manual isn't one book, it's ^numbered sections, and knowing that changes how useful it is. ^Section one is user commands. ^Section five is file formats. ^Section eight is administration. ^The same word can appear on several of those shelves. So |man passwd gives you the command that changes a password. But |man five passwd gives you ^the format of the etc passwd file, a completely different page answering a completely different question. ^The number in brackets at the top of any page tells you which one you're reading. ~If a manual page seems to be answering the wrong question, you're almost certainly on the wrong shelf. When a manual page seems to answer the wrong question, check the section number first.
headline: man passwd and man [5] passwd differ

narration: Here's the situation the manual normally fails at. ^You know exactly what you want to do, but you don't know what the command is called, ^and man needs a name you don't have. |Apropos solves it, because ^it searches the one-line descriptions of every manual page rather than their names. So ask it about disk usage and back come ^D U, which estimates file space usage, ^D F, which reports filesystem space, and ^N C D U, the interactive one. Three tools, from three different sections, found by describing the job. ^Man dash K is the identical command with a shorter name. ~Apropos answers the question you actually have, which is usually what was that thing called. Apropos is the command to remember for the days you've forgotten every other one.
headline: apropos searches [descriptions]

narration: The manual is complete, and completeness isn't always what you need at four in the afternoon. ^The page for tar runs to twelve hundred and forty one lines. ^T L D R's thorough and entirely correct. |T L D R, which stands for too long, didn't read, gives you ^eight lines instead: ^the handful of things people actually do with the command, written as examples you can copy. ^And what you wanted was almost certainly one of them. These aren't competitors. ^The manual is the reference you go to when the detail genuinely matters and you need to be sure. ^T L D R is the reminder you want when you've done this before and simply can't recall the flag order. ~Keep both. Install tldr today. T L D R'll save you the twelve hundred lines you didn't want to read. The manual settles arguments; tldr just gets you back to work.
headline: tldr gives you the [normal] usage

narration: There are three kinds of documentation and this is the third. ^The manual is written by the people who wrote the tool. ^T L D R is written by the community. |Cheat ^is written by you. ^Dash E opens your own sheet for a command, and ^whatever flag you keep forgetting gets written down once, ^then |recalled later exactly as you left it. That matters more than it sounds, because ^your notes can hold the details no general documentation ever will: your server names, your paths, the exact R sync incantation your deployment needs. ~Write it down the second time you look something up, because there's always a third time and you'll not remember then either. Your own notes, written once, beat re-reading somebody else's documentation three times.
headline: cheat stores [your own] notes

narration: A graphics card is installed, the machine boots perfectly well, and yet absolutely nothing on the system appears to be using the thing at all. |L S P C I dash K is where you find out why, because L S P C I lists hardware on the bus with the driver bound to each piece. ^The device is present, so the bus can see it. ^A kernel driver is in use, here i nine one five. ^Both of those need to be true. When ^that driver line is missing entirely, the hardware is present and completely unusable, and ^nothing will tell you: no error, no warning, it simply isn't used. ^That's a missing driver, not broken hardware, ^which is where an evening disappears. ~Present isn't working. Present and working are two different states, and lspci dash K is what tells them apart. Check the driver line before blaming the card, because that's where the evening goes.
headline: lspci shows the [driver] too

narration: Everything you plug in over U S B forms a physical tree, whether or not you ever picture it that way, and that shape explains a problem that otherwise makes no sense. |L S U S B dash T draws the tree. At the top sits ^bus one, the root hub on the motherboard. Into one port you've plugged ^an external hub, and hanging off it are ^a keyboard and ^an external drive. Here's what which tells you. ^Those two share one link back to the machine. ^The keyboard needs almost none of it; the drive would use all of it. So when ^that drive runs slowly and nothing about the drive changed, the answer is in this tree. Move it to ^a port on the machine, which has a link of its own. ~Nothing was broken; it was sharing. Before you replace a slow drive, look at the tree and try a different port. USB bandwidth is shared per hub, so where you plug something in genuinely matters.
headline: lsusb shows the [tree]

narration: Last one. You |know the job, not the command name. What do you reach for? Have a think, and pause here if you need longer. |Ready? Apropos, because it searches the descriptions.

quiz.question: Know the job, not the name. Reach for?
quiz.why: apropos searches descriptions, so the name is what it returns.

narration: And that's the bench, all |ten drawers filled. A hundred and nine tools, and you never have to memorise one, because you only need to know which drawer to open.

toolBench.headline: Ten drawers, [all filled]
toolBench.caption: You don't memorise tools. You learn the drawers.

narration: If one of these saved you a search, subscribing helps. And if you take one thing away, make it this: check what D D points at, twice, before you press enter.
